To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) in 23 human solid tumours of different origin, cultivation in soft agar selects for specific aneuploidy subpopulations, (2) this selection occurs during the early phase of cultivation in soft agar and (3) the selected subpopulations may differ with respect to ploidy as well
the DNA content of the cells forming colonies in soft agar may be different from that of the cells of the original tumours.

(1) in 8 of 23 human tumour cell populations, aneuploidy was selected during cultivation in softagar and (2) in 5 of 23 human diploid cell populations, an aneuploid population was selected during cultivation.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following topics: - the use of flow cytometry in the analysis of human solid tumours, - DNA content and S-phase fraction of human tumours, - selection of tumour cells during cultivation in softagar.

the following topics: 1) the effect of various growth factors on the proliferation of human tumours, 2) the effect of growth factors on the differentiation of human tumours and 3) the effect of tumour growth factors on normal cells.
the development of a novel, non-invasive method of monitoring the progression of human tumours.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the method of Courtenay & Mills (1978) is a very useful tool in the study of the biology and the chemosensitivity of human tumours.

in some human tumours cultivation in agar may select specific subpopulations of aneuploid cells, but in other cases the colonies contain a mixture of diploid and aneuploid or a purely diploid cell population.
the soft-agar assay is not a reliable method for the determination of the ploidy of human tumour cell populations in vivo.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in the majority of the cases, aneuploidy in tumours is not an accidental event, but is a stable feature of the tumour cell population.
the selection of tumour cells with specific DNA content during cultivation in soft-agar is a general phenomenon in human tumours.
in soft agar the tumour cells are able to proliferate and to select themselves according to their ploidy and proliferative activity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of soft agar for the isolation of tumor-initiating cells is not an unbiased method and that the selection of tumor-initiating cell subpopulations can be a major confounding factor.
the soft agar method can select specific aneupiloid tumour cell populations, which may not be present in the original cell population of a tumour.
the selection of aneuploid cells in soft agar is not a phenomenon limited to a specific histological type of cancer, but rather a common feature of a variety of human tumours.
